title: The covenant service
hook: the Methodist covenant prayer: put me to doing, put me to suffering
tomorrow: a hymn says the whole world would be too small a gift. for what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley's journal: an unwilling evening, and I felt my heart strangely warmed. Today, something Wesley gave his people to say out loud, together.
screen: `I FELT MY HEART.` → `SAID OUT LOUD, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Terms and conditions. Scroll, scroll, scroll, I agree. Nobody reads them; that's the joke. A covenant is the opposite: you read every line, out loud, in front of people, and you mean it. In the Methodist covenant service, a congregation says a prayer with a line in it that stops people mid-breath. Put me to doing, put me to suffering. So who would ever ask God to put them to suffering?
screen: `SCROLL, SCROLL, I AGREE.` → `A COVENANT, READ OUT LOUD.` → `PUT ME TO SUFFERING?`

segments.voice: Listen to how the prayer is built, and the puzzle undoes itself. It comes in pairs. Put me to doing, put me to suffering. Employed for you, or laid aside for you. Exalted, or brought low. Let me be full, let me be empty. Let me have all things, let me have nothing. Every pair has an easy half and a hard half. The prayer doesn't ask for the hard half. It hands over the choosing. Whichever half comes, the answer is the same, and it arrives near the end: I am thine. It's Paul's attitude in his letter to the Philippians, put into the mouth of a whole congregation: "every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need." Wesley drew the service from older Puritan writers and gave it to the Methodists, and Methodist churches still hold it, often near the new year. You can feel the pairs in your own two hands. A full hand grips. An empty hand opens. The prayer asks for neither one; it asks that both belong to God. One to tell a friend: the hardest-sounding line is half of a pair, and the other half is joy.
screen: `IT COMES IN PAIRS.` · `IT HANDS OVER THE CHOOSING.` · `BOTH TO BE FULL AND TO BE HUNGRY.` · `A FULL HAND, AN EMPTY HAND.` · then, large: `I AM THINE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees. Close one into a loose fist, full, and leave the other open, empty, palm up. Breathe in, and feel both; breathe out, and turn the fist slowly open to match the other. If you pray, the covenant's short line can go with that last breath: I am thine.
The covenant service. A Methodist congregation hands over the easy half and the hard half together, and ends: I am thine.
Your line: I am thine. Full hand or empty one, the prayer's answer doesn't change. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1663 COUNTS.` → `SAINTS AND TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 62 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: THE WHOLE WORLD, TOO SMALL A GIFT. FOR WHAT?`

howItsDone: Many Methodist churches hold a covenant service, often on the first Sunday of the year, when the congregation says the covenant prayer together; some Christians of other churches pray it privately.
